documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
64M here to establish. His longtime PCP is retiring at the end of the month and he wanted somebody he could reach by phone given everything going on.

HPI: A lot at once. Rectal bleeding in the spring led to a colonoscopy in July; rectal adenocarcinoma, staged IIIB. Oncology has him starting pelvic chemoradiation in September with surgery after. He is anxious about it but practical. Otherwise his chronic issues:
- DM2 on glargine 24 qHS and lispro 8 with meals plus a correction scale. Checks fingersticks 3-4x a day, mornings 130s-170s, no lows he can recall.
- Cirrhosis: hep C (genotype 1a) plus decades of drinking, diagnosed 2017 when he presented with fluid in the belly and confusion. Treated for hep C in 2018 by his hepatologist and was told it was cured. Has not had a drink since 2017. On furosemide 40 bid, spironolactone 100, lactulose (2-3 BMs a day, sometimes 4) and rifaximin. Hepatology sees him every 6 months with ultrasound.
- PAD: right fem-pop bypass in March of this year. Walks a few blocks.
- Venous disease left leg with a long-standing ulcer above the ankle; graft in May, partly taken. Wound clinic every few weeks. Pentoxifylline. Oxycodone 5 mg, usually 1-2 a day, for leg pain and achy knees/hands.
- COPD on tiotropium daily, albuterol a few times a week.
- Prostate cancer 2017: radical prostatectomy then radiation to the prostate bed. Urology checks PSA yearly, always undetectable or near it.
- CKD 3a per old labs. On aspirin, atorvastatin, amlodipine, metoprolol for his vascular disease.

PMH/PSH: as above. Prostatectomy 2017. R fem-pop 03/2020. L leg skin graft 05/2020.
Meds: reviewed bottle by bottle, 14 items, list reconciled.
Allergies: sulfa (rash). IV contrast dye (anaphylaxis, years ago with a CT).
FH: father died of pancreatic cancer at 72. Mother died at 78 of emphysema. Paternal uncle died of colon cancer at 68. One brother, treated for prostate cancer.
SH: Retired 2017 from the shipyard where he worked as a boiler tech. Smoked about 40 pack-years, quit 2017. Heavy drinker for about 30 years, none since 2017. No drugs.

ROS: fatigue, otherwise negative except as above.

Exam: Thin older man, no distress. Mild scleral icterus. Lungs: diminished breath sounds, no wheeze or crackles. Heart RRR, no murmur. Abd: soft, mildly protuberant, flanks dull, non-tender. Ext: healed R thigh/knee incisions; L lower leg with hemosiderin staining, graft site medial ankle with a small open area about 1.5 cm, clean base, dressing in place; trace edema. Pedal pulses diminished bilaterally. Feet: no other skin breakdown, monofilament intact. Neuro: alert, oriented, no asterixis.

A/P:
1. Rectal adenocarcinoma IIIB - oncology/radiation leading. We will be the home base; asked him to send any letters our way.
2. DM2 - A1c today. Same insulin.
3. Cirrhosis, decompensated - CMP, CBC, INR today; confirm HCV RNA negative since we have no paperwork. Continue diuretics, lactulose, rifaximin.
4. CKD 3a - BMP part of CMP, UACR.
5. PAD/venous ulcer - per vascular and wound clinic.
6. COPD - stable.
7. Health maintenance - HIV screen today (never done). Flu and pneumococcal next visit. Records requested from prior office and specialists.
Follow up 6 weeks.

Liver numbers (bilirubin, albumin, clotting) fit your known cirrhosis, nothing new. Blood count is slightly low, which we'll keep an eye on through treatment. No changes. See you in October.

MEDICAL ONCOLOGY — NEW PATIENT CONSULTATION
Date of service: 08/31/2020
Re: Peter Kimball, DOB 01/30/1956
Copy to: primary care physician

Reason: newly diagnosed rectal adenocarcinoma.

Mr. Kimball is a 64-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis (HCV, treated, and prior alcohol), insulin-treated diabetes, PAD and a 2017 prostatectomy with adjuvant prostate-bed radiation, who had hematochezia this spring. Colonoscopy 07/09/2020 found a mid-rectal mass; biopsies show moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. Pelvic MRI and staging imaging show regional nodal disease and no distant metastases: clinical stage IIIB.

Allergies: sulfonamides (rash); iodinated contrast (anaphylaxis) - staging done without iodinated contrast.

Assessment and plan: Locally advanced rectal cancer. We discussed long-course chemoradiation followed by resection. Radiation oncology has reviewed his prior prostate-bed fields and will plan around them. Concurrent capecitabine 1500 mg twice daily on radiation days, dose chosen with his liver function in mind; weekly CBC and CMP during treatment. Systemic chemotherapy beyond the radiosensitizing dose is not advisable with Child-Pugh C cirrhosis. Start 09/08/2020. Colorectal surgery referral for after completion.

Thank you for allowing us to share in his care.
Medical Oncology

documents.title: Pre-operative Evaluation
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Pre-op eval for LAR with diverting loop ileostomy planned 2/23 by colorectal surgery.

S: Turned 65 last month. Feels as well as he has in a while. Walks ~2 blocks before calf aching, unchanged since bypass. No chest pain, no exertional pressure, no syncope. Breathing at baseline, no recent exacerbation. Sugars ok. No confusion, 3 BMs/day.
O: Vitals as charted. Lungs diminished, no wheeze. Heart RRR no murmur. Abd soft, mild shifting dullness, NT. L ankle ulcer small and clean. ECG: NSR, normal.
A/P: Elevated but accepted risk, driven by liver disease (Child-Pugh C) more than heart or lungs. No active cardiac conditions; functional capacity limited by claudication rather than angina; no further cardiac testing would change management.
- Continue aspirin per surgeon's preference (they asked to keep it), metoprolol and statin through surgery.
- Hold amlodipine morning of surgery if SBP low.
- Insulin: glargine 80% (19 units) the night before; hold lispro while NPO, correction scale in hospital.
- Diuretics: hold morning of surgery; hepatology aware.
- Continue lactulose/rifaximin post-op as soon as he can take PO; watch for encephalopathy with opioids.
- No iodinated contrast - anaphylaxis.
Letter faxed to surgeon.

documents.title: Discharge Summary - Colorectal Surgery
documents.author: colorectal surgery
documents.body:
Admission 02/23/2021 - Discharge 03/01/2021
Procedure 02/23/2021: low anterior resection with diverting loop ileostomy.
Indication: stage IIIB rectal adenocarcinoma after neoadjuvant chemoradiation.
Course: Uncomplicated operation. Post-op ileus resolved day 3. Ascites managed with resumption of home diuretics on day 2; no paracentesis needed. Lactulose resumed on day 2 at a reduced dose and opioids kept to a minimum; no confusion. Glucose managed with basal insulin plus correction. Ileostomy functioning, output 800-1200 mL/day at discharge. Stoma nurse teaching completed.
Pathology: residual adenocarcinoma, margins negative (see report).
Discharge medications: home list resumed unchanged; lactulose dose per ostomy output (aim for no confusion, not a set number of BMs).
Allergies: sulfonamides, iodinated contrast.
Follow-up: colorectal clinic 2 weeks; oncology 4 weeks; PCP 2-3 weeks. Reversal planned in about 6 months. No adjuvant chemotherapy recommended given liver function.

documents.title: Pulmonology Consultation
documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
PULMONARY MEDICINE CONSULTATION
Date of service: 08/25/2022
Re: Peter Kimball, 66
Referring: primary care

He describes about six months of breathlessness that has steadily worsened, along with a dry cough. Decades of work in a shipyard as a boiler technician; he recalls insulation dust everywhere in the early years. Retired 2017. Former smoker, 40 pack-years, quit 2017. Known COPD on tiotropium and as-needed albuterol.
Allergies: sulfonamides, iodinated contrast (anaphylaxis).

Exam: clubbing of the fingers. Crackles at the end of inspiration over both lung bases. No wheeze. No accessory muscle use at rest.

Chest radiograph today: fibrotic change in both lower lobes, pleural thickening and calcified pleural plaques.
PFTs today: decreased TLC, FVC and DLCO with a normal FEV1 and a normal FEV1/FVC ratio - restriction with impaired gas transfer.

Impression: asbestosis (asbestos-related pneumoconiosis) with pleural plaque disease, explaining the progressive dyspnea and cough.
Plan: continue current inhalers. Counseled on the diagnosis, the relationship to his occupational exposure and the slow natural history. Repeat PFTs in 6-12 months. Vaccinations up to date per patient. Return sooner for worsening.

documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
GASTROENTEROLOGY, 12/12/2022
Reason for visit: rectal bleeding and changed bowel habits.

Mr. Kimball, 66, had long-course pelvic chemoradiation for stage IIIB rectal adenocarcinoma, finishing about two years ago, followed by low anterior resection; he also had prostate-bed radiation in 2017. For roughly six months he has passed blood per rectum and has had more urgency, with some episodes of fecal incontinence.
Allergies: sulfonamides, iodinated contrast.

Exam: well-appearing. Digital rectal exam: firm, non-tender rectum, no mass felt.
Labs today: Hgb 10.2, MCV 92, WBC 7.0, platelets 250.

Colonoscopy (same day): numerous telangiectatic vessels in the rectum, oozing on contact. Anastomosis intact. No mass, ulcer or other mucosal lesion to suggest recurrent cancer. Argon plasma coagulation applied to the telangiectasias in the rectum with good hemostasis.

Impression: chronic radiation proctitis with bleeding causing normocytic anemia; no recurrence.
Plan: APC can be repeated if bleeding recurs. CBC in 4-6 weeks with PCP. Avoid straining; continue lactulose titration.
Gastroenterology

DERMATOLOGY CONSULTATION, 06/07/2023
Referred by primary care for a left lower-leg ulcer.

History: diabetic with peripheral arterial and venous disease, recently seen by pulmonology and gastroenterology. The ulcer on his left lower leg has been open for more than two years in spite of grafting; over recent months it has grown and become more painful. He has had no fever or chills.
Allergies: sulfonamides, iodinated contrast.

Exam: on the left medial lower leg, a 3 cm ulcer whose edges are raised and everted; the base bleeds easily when touched. The surrounding skin is indurated, with several keratotic areas. No palpable inguinal or popliteal lymph nodes. Remainder of the skin and general exam unremarkable.

Data: A1c 7.8%, fasting glucose 172 mg/dL, CBC unremarkable (drawn this week). Ankle-brachial index 0.7 on the left.

Procedure: punch biopsy from the ulcer edge, after consent; hemostasis with pressure; dressing.

Impression: chronic ulcer with features worrying for malignant transformation (Marjolin ulcer); also arterial insufficiency on the left contributes to poor healing.
Plan: biopsy pending; will call patient and PCP.
Dermatology

documents.title: Hepatology visit letter
documents.author: hepatology
documents.body:
HEPATOLOGY, 12/01/2023
Dear colleague,
Thank you for moving Mr. Kimball up. He returns, now 67, with three months of increasing fatigue, a swelling abdomen and a 10-lb weight loss; he denies fever, chills or sweats. Background: decompensated cirrhosis (HCV cured 2018, prior alcohol), radiation proctitis after rectal cancer treatment, and a squamous cell carcinoma of the leg excised this summer.

Exam: cachectic. Jaundice of skin and sclerae. Distended abdomen with a fluid wave. A firm, irregular mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant.

Labs: Hgb 11.2, platelets 85, INR 1.6, total bilirubin 3.2, albumin 2.9, AST 80, ALT 75, alkaline phosphatase 120, AFP 400 ng/mL (previously under 10).
Ultrasound today: 5 cm heterogeneous, nodular mass in the right lobe; no biliary obstruction; moderate ascites.

Impression: suspected hepatocellular carcinoma on a background of Child-Pugh C cirrhosis.
Plan:
1. Multiphase MRI with gadolinium (anaphylaxis was to iodinated contrast) to characterize the lesion.
2. Referral to the transplant center: a single lesion of this size would fall within transplant criteria, and his liver function argues for transplant over other treatment.
3. Diuretics unchanged; diagnostic paracentesis not needed today (no fever, no pain).
I will copy you on the MRI.
Hepatology

LIVER TRANSPLANT PROGRAM, 02/20/2024
Re: Peter Kimball, 68
Mr. Kimball was seen to begin liver transplant evaluation for hepatocellular carcinoma (single 5.0 cm LI-RADS 5 lesion, AFP 400) in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis from treated hepatitis C and prior alcohol use, abstinent since 2017.

GASTROENTEROLOGY, 08/23/2024
Mr. Kimball comes back to us, nine months after his hepatology diagnosis of HCC, with intermittent abdominal pain and continued weight loss. Over two weeks his left arm veins were tender and red and then settled on their own; now the same thing has started over the right side of his chest. Background: radiation proctitis (APC 12/2022), Child-Pugh C cirrhosis, HCC under transplant evaluation.
Family history: father died of pancreatic adenocarcinoma at 72; paternal uncle colorectal cancer; brother prostate cancer; mother emphysema.
Social: 40 pack-years, quit 2017; no alcohol since 2017.
Allergies: sulfonamides, iodinated contrast.

Exam: along the superficial veins of the right chest wall, a palpable cord with redness and tenderness. Abdomen soft, not distended, no masses, no enlargement of liver or spleen on my exam.

Labs: Hgb 12.1, WBC 7.8, platelets 305, fasting glucose 156, CA 19-9 120 U/mL, CEA 5.2 ng/mL.

Impression: migratory superficial thrombophlebitis with a raised CA 19-9 and weight loss - concerning for an occult pancreatic malignancy (Trousseau phenomenon), especially with his father's history.
Plan: MRI abdomen with gadolinium (pancreas protocol; no iodinated contrast), then EUS with FNA of any lesion.
Gastroenterology

documents.title: Oncology consultation - pancreatic cancer
documents.author: oncology
documents.body:
MEDICAL ONCOLOGY, 09/26/2024
Mr. Kimball is known to us from his rectal cancer. EUS-FNA of a 2.6 cm pancreatic body mass shows adenocarcinoma; CA 19-9 120. He also has a 5 cm HCC in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis (bilirubin about 3, albumin under 3, INR 1.5-1.6).
Assessment: pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Resection is not possible with his liver disease, and standard chemotherapy regimens are not safe with Child-Pugh C function and this bilirubin. We talked at length; he understands the treatment options are limited and wants to focus on staying as well as he can.
Plan: supportive care, symptom management, oncology visits every 2-3 months with CA 19-9 and imaging as needed. We will let the transplant program know. Palliative care resources discussed and offered.

documents.title: Oncology visit - back pain
documents.author: oncology
documents.body:
MEDICAL ONCOLOGY, 03/05/2025
Thank you for the heads-up about his back. Mr. Kimball, with pancreatic adenocarcinoma, HCC and a history of rectal and prostate cancers, returns with three months of dull low-back pain that is worse at night and does not ease with rest.
Exam: focal tenderness over the T10 spinous process. Mild weakness of both legs. Light-touch sensation reduced below the level of the umbilicus. Rectal tone not tested.
Labs: calcium 11.2 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 140 U/L, PSA 0.2 ng/mL, Hgb 12.5 g/dL.
MRI thoracic spine the same afternoon (no contrast): T10 metastasis with an epidural component contacting the cord, no cord signal change, no fracture.

Impression: metastatic carcinoma to bone at T10 with epidural extension and early neurologic signs; hypercalcemia of malignancy. Most likely pancreatic in origin; PSA remains low, making prostate unlikely. Biopsy would not change treatment and was not pursued.
Plan:
1. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV today, then 4 mg every 6 hours with a taper over four weeks.
2. Urgent radiation oncology: palliative radiation to T10 begins tomorrow, 30 Gy in 10 fractions.
3. Zoledronic acid 3.5 mg IV (dose adjusted for kidney function) tomorrow, then every 12 weeks. Oral hydration.
4. Glucose will rise on steroids - he will use his correction-scale lispro; PCP copied.
5. Return immediately for worse weakness, numbness or incontinence.
Medical Oncology

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT RECORD, 09/02/2025 (received with hospital records)
CC: right upper quadrant pain, fever and vomiting.
HPI: 69-year-old man with pancreatic adenocarcinoma metastatic to bone, HCC and decompensated cirrhosis from hepatitis C. For 24 hours, severe right upper abdominal pain, constant and sharp, going through to the right shoulder, with fever and repeated vomiting.

documents.title: Discharge summary - cholecystitis
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 09/02/2025, discharged 09/08/2025.
Diagnosis: acute emphysematous cholecystitis with cholelithiasis.
Background: pancreatic adenocarcinoma with bone metastasis, HCC, Child-Pugh C cirrhosis, CKD 3a, insulin-treated diabetes.
Course: Surgery judged him too high risk for cholecystectomy given Child-Pugh C cirrhosis and metastatic cancer, in line with his stated wishes. Interventional radiology placed a percutaneous cholecystostomy tube under ultrasound guidance on 09/03. IV piperacillin-tazobactam continued; fever settled by 09/05 and pain improved. Diet advanced. Lactulose and rifaximin continued; no encephalopathy. Insulin adjusted while eating little, back to home doses at discharge.
Discharge medications: home medications unchanged, plus amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily to complete 14 days of antibiotics (through 09/16).
Drain: flush daily, record output. IR follow-up in 6 weeks for cholangiogram and possible removal.
Code status: DNR/DNI per patient.
Follow-up: IR, oncology, PCP.

documents.title: Discharge summary - C. difficile colitis with toxic megacolon
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 03/06/2026 - discharged 03/20/2026. ICU 03/09 - 03/13.
Principal diagnosis: Clostridioides difficile infection complicated by toxic megacolon.
Presentation: 70-year-old man (pancreatic adenocarcinoma with bone metastasis, HCC, Child-Pugh C cirrhosis, chronic radiation proctitis, emphysematous cholecystitis in September) with five days of watery diarrhea, cramping abdominal pain and low-grade fever, two weeks after completing clindamycin for pneumonia. Admission vitals: T 38.2 C (100.8 F), BP 110/70, HR 102, RR 22. WBC 18.0, Hgb 13.2, platelets 250, creatinine 1.2, BUN 28. Stool C. difficile toxin positive. Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily started 03/06.
Hospital course: On the third day of vancomycin his diarrhea stopped, but he became more lethargic, with fever to 39.4 C (102.9 F) and heart rate 120. Abdomen distended and diffusely tender without rebound or guarding; bowel sounds hypoactive. Repeat WBC 25.0. Abdominal radiograph: marked colonic distension without free air. Transferred to the ICU 03/09 with toxic megacolon. Treated as fulminant C. difficile: vancomycin 500 mg four times daily by nasogastric tube, vancomycin retention enemas, IV metronidazole 500 mg every 8 hours, bowel rest, IV fluids. General surgery consulted daily; given his Child-Pugh C cirrhosis, metastatic cancer and stated wishes (DNR/DNI, would accept treatment aimed at returning home), colectomy was not pursued while he improved. Distension resolved on serial films by 03/12; returned to the floor 03/13. Diet resumed; stools formed by discharge. WBC 9.6 on 03/20. No encephalopathy; lactulose held in the ICU and resumed at a lower dose, then back to his home titration.
Discharge medications: home medications unchanged; vancomycin 125 mg by mouth four times daily through 03/31/2026.
Allergies: sulfonamides, iodinated contrast. Add: avoid clindamycin if possible.
Follow-up: PCP and oncology in 1-2 weeks; return for recurrent diarrhea, fever or abdominal swelling.

documents.title: Reply
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Thanks for the update, Peter. The PCP has read your hospital records. Finish the vancomycin, and call us the same day if you have watery diarrhea again, fever or a swollen belly - C. diff can come back after treatment. We'll leave a follow-up up to you; just call when you'd like to be seen.
